title: US Student Loan Defaults Hit $234 Billion — and Collections May Restart
excerpt: Federal data through June 30 shows 9.3 million borrowers in default — up from 7.7 million six months earlier — as the Trump administration keeps involuntary collections paused while it stands up a new support system.
body:
• The numbers: 9.3 million federal borrowers are in default on $234 billion in loans as of June 30, 2026 — roughly 14% of the $1.64 trillion federally managed portfolio, up from 7.7 million borrowers and $180 billion just six months earlier.
  • What default costs you: When involuntary collections resume, borrowers face wage garnishment of up to 15% of disposable pay, seizure of federal tax refunds through the Treasury Offset Program, and collection costs of up to 24% of the loan balance — plus the default line on their credit report.
  • Collections are paused — for now: Since January 16, 2026, the Department of Education has paused wage garnishment and tax offsets while it rolls out new repayment options, including the Repayment Assistance Plan launched July 1. No restart date has been announced, but borrowers in default should expect a 65-day written notice before any offset resumes.
  • Your way out: Loan rehabilitation — nine consecutive income-based payments — removes the default line from your credit report entirely; consolidation and income-driven plans are alternatives. A new Defaulted Loans Support Center on StudentAid.gov now lets borrowers compare options and apply online instead of by mail or fax.

America's student loan crisis has reached a milestone no one wanted. Federal data released September 22 by Federal Student Aid show that 9.3 million borrowers are now in default on $234 billion in federal student loans — the highest share in the program's history, according to borrowers' advocates. That is roughly one in five federal borrowers, and the defaulted balance now equals about 14% of the $1.64 trillion portfolio the Education Department manages directly.

The six-month trend tells the story. When FSA released its December 2025 numbers in March, 7.7 million borrowers held $180 billion in defaulted loans. The defaulted portfolio has since added about 1.6 million borrowers and $54 billion — and senators pressed the department last week over its handling of a $1 billion servicing fund amid the surge.

Context & Background

The current pileup traces back to the pandemic. In March 2020, the federal government paused student loan payments for the first time in the program's history, then extended the pause repeatedly. The moratorium technically ended in January 2024, but a nine-month on-ramp extension ran through September 2024 — and missed payments didn't reach credit reports in full force until early 2025.

Betsy Mayotte, founder and president of The Institute of Student Loan Advisors, describes the result as a perfect storm. Borrowers who had been in the habit of making payments were taken out of that habit for years, then returned to repayment into an economy where healthcare, housing, and food costs had all climbed. The Biden-era SAVE plan — which had given 7.5 million borrowers reduced payments — was terminated by a federal appeals court, leaving many facing sharply higher bills on budgets built around the lower payments.

"Defaulting is almost always more expensive for you, both monthly and in the long term, than trying to find a way to afford one of the payment options available to federal student loan borrowers."

— Betsy Mayotte, Founder and President, The Institute of Student Loan Advisors

Younger borrowers are taking a disproportionate hit. About one in four people who graduated since 2020 are now 90 days or more past due — and those missed payments are damaging their credit just as they try to rent apartments and finance cars.

Impact & Analysis

Default is far more than a credit-score problem. Once a federal loan passes 270 days without payment, the full unpaid balance becomes immediately due, and the borrower loses eligibility for further federal aid and deferment. When involuntary collections are running, the government can garnish up to 15% of disposable pay directly from the paycheck — more than most income-driven plans would take, and off gross pay rather than income minus a family-size allowance. Tax refunds and portions of Social Security benefits can be seized, and collection costs of up to 24% get tacked onto the balance.

That collections machinery is currently idle. On January 16, the Department of Education paused involuntary collections — administrative wage garnishment and Treasury offsets — to give defaulted borrowers time to use the new repayment options rolling out under the department's overhaul, including the Repayment Assistance Plan that launched July 1, 2026. The pause is temporary, and the department has not announced a restart date. In 2019, the last year offsets ran at full scale, about 1.4 million tax refunds were seized.

The stakes extend beyond individual balance sheets. Borrowers earning under $50,000 fall behind at nearly three times the rate of those earning $100,000 or more, according to Federal Reserve data, and about one in five borrowers overall is behind. When 9.3 million households lose up to 15% of their paychecks, the drag on consumer spending is material.

Diaspora Angle

Indian students are among the largest borrowers financing US graduate education through federal loans where eligible, and many carry that debt through OPT and H-1B years. Default carries extra jeopardy for visa-holding graduates: wage garnishment hits the same paycheck that funds visa renewals and green-card applications, and damaged credit complicates apartment leases and auto financing in exactly the years a new immigrant is establishing a financial footprint. The July 2026 repayment-plan changes and the new online support center apply regardless of citizenship — any federal-loan borrower can use them.

What's Next

The immediate question is when the collections pause ends. The department says it wants defaulted borrowers using the new Repayment Assistance Plan and the revamped online system before garnishments resume — and the newly launched Defaulted Loans Support Center, built jointly by the Education Department and Treasury on StudentAid.gov, is the centerpiece of that effort. It replaces decades-old mail-and-fax processes with an online portal where borrowers can compare rehabilitation versus consolidation, apply, and make payments.

For borrowers in default, the arithmetic is unforgiving. Rehabilitation requires nine consecutive payments based on income, after which the default line comes off the credit report as if it never existed. Consolidation gets the loan current faster but leaves the history in place. Either way, advocates say, acting during the pause beats waiting for the garnishment notices — because when offsets resume, the government only has to mail a 65-day notice before taking the refund.
